passages.t: Micah's silver and his mother's idol
passages.happening:
A man named Micah, from the hill country of Ephraim, tells his mother that the eleven hundred shekels of silver stolen from her, over which he heard her speak a curse, are with him. He took them. His mother answers, “Blessed be my son by the LORD!” (verses 1-2).

He gives the silver back. She says, “I wholly dedicate the silver to the LORD for my son’s benefit, to make a graven image and a molten idol” (verse 3). She takes two hundred shekels to a silversmith, who makes the idol, and it is put in Micah's house (verse 4).

Micah has a shrine. He makes an ephod and household idols and appoints one of his own sons as his priest (verse 5).

“In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The judges are gone. The last five chapters of the book tell two stories, and this is the first. It is short, and it is heavy with irony.

Micah's name means who is like the LORD, and in the first verses it is written in a longer form that includes the name of God. Yet his house is full of idols.

People believed that a curse spoken over stolen goods had real power, which may be why Micah owns up once he hears his mother's curse. She answers with words of favor in the LORD's name. Then she dedicates the silver to the LORD, and uses part of it to make an idol. She keeps most of the rest. Faith in the LORD and the ways of the neighbors had become thoroughly mixed.

The second commandment forbade any carved image for worship. The law even pronounced a curse on anyone who made one and set it up in secret.

The items in Micah's shrine are known from the Old Testament and its world. The carved image and the cast idol may be one object, a carved image covered in metal, or two. An ephod was a priestly garment, and in some places an object used to seek guidance. The household idols, called teraphim in Hebrew, were small figures kept in the home, perhaps linked with family ancestors or used to seek guidance. Rachel stole her father's.

Only the descendants of Aaron were to serve as priests. Micah makes his own son a priest in his own house.

Then the narrator gives his only comment, at the center of the chapter, and it explains everything around it. There was no king, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes. The word for right usually describes what is right in the LORD's eyes. Now each person's own eyes are the measure.
passages.later:
Moses had warned against exactly this: “You are not to do as we are doing here today, where everyone does what seems right in his own eyes” (Deuteronomy 12:8). The law said, “You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath” (Exodus 20:4).

The household idols appear in Genesis too: “Rachel stole her father’s household idols” (Genesis 31:19).
passages.asks: Micah's mother dedicated her silver to the LORD and then made an idol with it. Ask where you mix real devotion to God with ways of worship he has never asked for. And ask whose eyes decide what is right in your life, God's or your own.

passages.happening:
There is a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah. He leaves Bethlehem to settle wherever he can find a place, and on his travels he comes to Micah's house (verses 7-8).

Micah asks where he is from. “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah,” he replied, “and I am on my way to settle wherever I can find a place” (verse 9).

“Stay with me,” Micah said to him, “and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions” (verse 10). The Levite agrees, and he becomes like a son to Micah (verse 11). Micah appoints him, and the young man becomes his priest and lives in his house (verse 12).

Then Micah says, “Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve at the sanctuary. They received no share of land of their own. Instead they were given towns scattered among the tribes, and they lived on the tithes and offerings of the people. A Levite wandering in search of a living suggests that this way of providing for them was breaking down, perhaps because Israel was neglecting its tithes. Bethlehem was not one of the Levites' towns, which is another sign that things were not ordered as the law intended.

Micah's offer of ten shekels a year, clothing and food was a respectable wage for the time. He hires a priest the way one would hire a craftsman.

He ordained his own son first. Now he replaces him with a Levite, as if a better qualification would improve the arrangement.

His last words are the reader's key: ‘Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest.’ Micah believes he has secured God's favor through the right religious professional. The reader knows better. A shrine full of idols, served by a hired priest, is not made pleasing to God by the priest's family tree.

Bethlehem will appear again in chapter 19, and in the book of Ruth. Some readers see in these mentions the book's quiet interest in the town that would give Israel King David.
passages.later:
The law gave the priesthood to Aaron's family: “So you shall appoint Aaron and his sons to carry out the duties of the priesthood” (Numbers 3:10). And a Levite who wished to serve was to come ‘to the place the LORD will choose’ (Deuteronomy 18:6), not to a private shrine.

The books of Samuel tell how Bethlehem became the town of King David (1 Samuel 16:1).
passages.asks: Micah thought the right priest would guarantee God's goodness. Ask whether you have ever tried to secure God's favor through the right church, the right leader or the right practice, more than through turning to him. And ask what you would do if no one were watching and no one could tell you otherwise.
